events.summary: A contributor proposes turning on autoDestroy for IncomingMessage and replacing manual destroy and close handling in the HTTP client and server with the standard stream destroy.
A maintainer says IncomingMessage's custom destroy override blocks this and must be fixed first.
The opener agrees to look into it and notes keep-alive sockets must not be destroyed.
The opener reports that removing the override fixes resets but causes double close events and hangs.
The opener marks the PR ready for review.
The opener notes the change overrides a maintainer's recent work and is unsure the approach is best.
A maintainer pings a colleague to review.
A maintainer says the destroy callback must always be called or state gets corrupted.
A maintainer requests changes, asking to remove all manual destroyed and close handling rather than keep a hybrid.
The opener agrees and asks whether he may change the server code.
The opener asks whether existing abort behaviour must be kept, suggests a custom destroy rather than the shared one, and proposes an abort method.
A maintainer says to keep the behaviour inside a regular destroy, rejects a custom implementation, and rejects an abort method since abort was just deprecated on requests.
The opener agrees and notes the only difference is that errors are emitted only when listeners exist.
A maintainer offers to help and suggests commenting out tests that depend on that behaviour for now.
The opener moves abort logic into destroy with a readableEnded check.
The opener notes a client code path may be unnecessary after the change.
The opener says the change breaks a test for aborted behaviour and asks which way to go.
The opener wonders whether the standard destroy could regress performance.
The opener reports excluding tests that rely on the error-event behaviour and moving aborted emission into destroy.
A maintainer praises progress and promises help later.
The opener asks whether to keep emitting errors only when listeners exist or to change tests for a breaking change.
The opener says he chose to preserve the old behaviour.
The opener shows a failing test and asks whether that is acceptable or a custom destroy is needed.
The opener lists a third option: a custom destroy that emits errors only when listeners are attached.
The opener clarifies he is asking whether the test can be changed.
A maintainer firmly rejects swallowing errors that way.
The opener agrees to write a destroy that keeps the server's previous logic.
The opener explains the new approach is backward compatible but checks listeners on every error, not only on early termination.
The opener asks which benchmark to run.
A maintainer says destroy performance is not a concern.
A bot posts a coverage report.
The opener asks whether the work is on the right track.
A maintainer says it looks good and asks if it is ready.
The opener says it is ready apart from one open doubt and a new macOS failure.
A maintainer suggests doing the listener check inside the branch that emits aborted.
A maintainer labels the PR semver-major.
A maintainer says the slight timing change makes it semver-major.
A maintainer asks whether the socket should only be destroyed on abort and wants a comment.
A maintainer sketches a destroy implementation that waits for the socket to finish.
The opener asks why the callback should wait for the socket.
A maintainer says waiting is best practice but optional.
The opener thanks him.
The opener reports the sketch breaks tests that destroy without an error and one where the finished callback never fires, and shares a variant.
The opener debugs why the finished callback never runs on the client.
The opener checks for an already destroyed socket and asks for review.
A maintainer says the destroyed check should be unnecessary.
A maintainer suggests a variable rename.
The opener explains a test hits an already destroyed socket.
A maintainer suggests the finished helper may need fixing.
A maintainer asks for an explanatory comment.
A maintainer asks about test status.
The opener agrees.
The opener reports all tests pass with unchanged behaviour apart from timing.
The opener notes no tests needed changing.
A maintainer approves.
A maintainer requests CI.
A maintainer proposes landing on v15 but not v14 and asks the HTTP team and TSC for views.
A maintainer asks whether destroy could always default to an aborted error.
A bot clears the CI request label.
A bot posts the CI run link.
The opener says tests expect no error event when destroy gets no error.
A maintainer defers that to a possible future major.
A second maintainer approves and agrees.
A maintainer labels it not to land on v14.
A maintainer labels it not to land on v12.
A maintainer labels it not to land on v10.
A maintainer removes the semver-major label.
A maintainer relabels it semver-minor.
A maintainer flags a stray whitespace change as non-blocking.
A maintainer approves.
The opener will fix it.
An outside reviewer says the listener check now swallows all errors, not only abort errors, and suggests a narrower condition.
The opener agrees to the stricter check.
The outside reviewer suggests conventional argument order.
The opener agrees.
The opener says the old code was not that strict and asks for a pointer.
A maintainer sides with the outside reviewer.
A maintainer says destroying with an error and no listener should be an uncaught exception.
A maintainer asks for a test.
The opener concedes and will fix and test it.
A maintainer requests CI.
A bot clears the CI request label.
A bot posts the CI run link.
The opener reports the fix.
The opener asks about testing that the process crashes.
A maintainer suggests an uncaught exception handler.
The opener thanks him.
The opener finds error propagation on this branch differs from the current release and shows output.
The opener notes destroy no longer always emits an abort error and needs fixing.
The opener reopens the thread, arguing the old code only emitted errors in abort paths and errors did not bubble from response to request, and adds tests.
A maintainer requests CI.
A bot clears the CI request label.
A bot posts the CI run link.
A maintainer adds the commit-queue label.
A bot removes the commit-queue label.
A bot reports the commits landed.
A bot closes the PR after landing.
A maintainer celebrates the fix.
The opener thanks everyone.
A maintainer links the v15.5.0 release that included it.
A framework author reports it breaks hapi by emitting close on the request before the response is sent, and says this contradicts docs and is semver-major.
A maintainer says the docs were wrong but agrees early close is breaking even if more correct.
A maintainer suggests reverting on v15 and asks the opener for a regression test on close ordering.
The opener agrees to write the test.
The framework author agrees it is more correct but breaking, and explains why tests missed it.
The opener proposes an existing test file and asks about expected ordering.
The framework author says that test misses the case and gives a reproduction.
The opener sees the difference.
A maintainer says it should be reverted in v15.
The opener apologises.
A release maintainer relabels it semver-major.
A release maintainer removes the semver-minor label.
A release maintainer asks for a revert PR on the v15 staging branch.
A maintainer reassures the opener.
The opener links a PR adding a close-ordering test.
A maintainer asks the opener to open the revert.
A maintainer asks releasers to note the change in v16 release notes.
The opener agrees and asks how to revert the commits.
A release maintainer adds the notable-change label.
The opener links a first revert PR.
The opener links the revert PR for v15.
The opener posts the revert PR link.
A hapi maintainer links a hapi change to rely on response close for Node 16.
A maintainer links a later PR documenting the breaking change.
A user links a later doc fix on HTTP event order.
A user asks years later how client aborts were meant to be detected after this change and whether to document the current way or restore the abort event.
